page_checks.summary: Contents page lists section titles and page numbers but contains no grammatical exposition.
Contents page lists section titles and page numbers but contains no grammatical exposition.
The clause is analysed in terms of predicator, complements and adjuncts; the recursive auxiliary analysis differs from a single verb-group view.
Canonical clause patterns distinguish subject, objects, predicative complements and oblique PP complements; core and noncore divide is not simply transitivity.
Lexical transitivity can vary by verb use; subject-oriented and object-oriented predicative complements have different predicands.
Copular clauses are defined narrowly with be; predicative complements and finite content-clause complements are distinct structures.
Valency counts syntactic complements and is compared with transitivity in a table; complement licensing by the head begins the complement–adjunct comparison.
Verb subcategorisation can select a preposition or a subordinate clause type; alternate prepositions can alter meaning rather than always cause ungrammaticality.
Selected dependent clauses versus optional adjunct clauses, obligatory objects with peruse versus optional ones with read, and the difference between licensing and obligatoriness.
Required and optional locative complements and passive by-phrases, with exceptions for broad copular-be complements; do-so anaphora is introduced.
The do-so test diagnoses complement versus adjunct status, with counterexamples and limitations; phrases and adjuncts have distinct categories/functions.
NPs can be time/manner adjuncts; adverbs can be selected complements; PPs can be complements or adjuncts; PP subordinates vary by construction.
Subordinate clauses and AdjPs occur as complements or adjuncts; typical linear positions and mobility provide a nonabsolute diagnostic.
Syntactic complements and semantic arguments are not identical; expletives and raising are distinguished without derivational movement requirements.
Semantic selection restrictions can create anomalies distinct from grammatical ill-formedness; role labels depend on semantic predicates.
PP roles can depend jointly on the verb and preposition; semantic roles are introduced at different levels of specificity.
Semantic role differs from presentational status; active/passive, symmetric and converse predicates illustrate multiple role–function alignments.
Converse buy/sell and precede/follow express alternative perspectives; causer and prototypical agent are introduced.
Agentivity depends on verb, animation and volition; purpose can force agentive interpretation; instrument differs from causer and patient.
Emotion, perception and cognition use experiencer–stimulus relations; themes cover motion, location, transfer and property change.
